key_insight: Large language models can identify subjective, context-dependent text spans but produce variable outputs; targeted prompting and calibration improve consistency and alignment with human judgments.
problem_solved: Evaluates how well LLMs handle subjective span identification—a challenging, ambiguity-prone task unlike explicit NER—and provides practical strategies and metrics to improve reliability and interpretability.
method: Benchmark multiple LLMs and smaller pre-trained models on curated subjective-span datasets and tasks.
Compare prompting strategies (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought) and apply post-processing/calibration to stabilize outputs.
Measure model–human agreement, consistency, and document annotation guidelines and evaluation criteria for subjective spans.
impact: Provides practitioners with concrete guidance for using and tuning LLMs in explainability and information-extraction settings where spans are subjective, helping choose trade-offs between model size, cost, and reliability. Improves annotation and evaluation practices for downstream NLP tasks that rely on interpretability.
visual_elements: Annotated example panel showing a sentence with multiple plausible subjective spans and model outputs side-by-side
Bar chart comparing model–human agreement and confidence across models and prompting strategies
Pipeline diagram: prompt design → LLM extraction → calibration/post-processing → evaluation
Heatmap of inter-annotator agreement vs. model agreement to highlight subjective regions
paper_title: Exploring the Performance of Large Language Models on Subjective Span Identification Tasks
paper_authors: Alphaeus Dmonte, Roland Oruche, Tharindu Ranasinghe, Marcos Zampieri, Prasad Calyam
